title: Counting — and four ways to attach a number
goal: Count from zero to a million, give your age and phone number — and install the rule that trips up almost every learner: nouns change form according to the NUMBER in front of them, in four different patterns.
bekal: say the numbers 0-100 and recognize the back-to-front order of *enaindvajset* (one-and-twenty)
choose the noun form according to the number: 1, 2, 3-4, and 5 and up
give your age with *star sem … let* and ask about quantities with *koliko*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — V knjižnici
dialogs.intro: Budi is signing up at the city library. The librarian is patient, and accidentally gives him an important grammar lesson.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nič štiri ena, dve tri, pet šest sedem.
lines.id: Zero four one, two three, five six seven.
lines.literal: zero four one, two three, five six seven.

lines.speaker: Uslužbenka:
lines.id: Thank you. How many books would you like?

lines.speaker: Uslužbenka:
lines.text: Ker je pet. Do štiri je drugače.
lines.id: Because it's five. Up to four it's different.
lines.literal: because is five. up-to four is different.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Torej dve knjigi, tri knjige, pet knjig?
lines.id: So dve knjigi, tri knjige, pet knjig?
lines.literal: so two books-two, three books-pl, five of-books?

lines.speaker: Uslužbenka:
lines.id: Exactly. Now you know how to count.

notes: **Age is measured, not owned.** Slovenian doesn't say "I have 23 years" (like French or Spanish), and it doesn't just say "I'm 23" (like English). It says *Star sem triindvajset let* — "I am old by twenty-three years". A woman says *Stara sem*, because *star* is an adjective and adjectives follow gender.

**Triindvajset = three-and-twenty.** Numbers 21 to 99 are said back to front: the ones first, then *in* (and), then the tens. It's exactly how German and Dutch do it (and old English "four-and-twenty blackbirds") — no coincidence, given Slovenia's long history under Vienna.

**Nič for zero, but not always in phone numbers.** When counting, zero is *nič*. Reading out phone numbers, Slovenians also often use *nula*. Notice too that phone numbers are read in small groups, and the two comes out as *dve* — habit, not a rule.

**Koliko always pulls in the Genitive.** *Koliko knjig?* (how many books?), *Koliko ljudi?* (how many people?), *Koliko časa?* (how long?). That form is the same as the one after five and up, so once you've mastered one, you've mastered both.

**Za tri tedne — the number three takes the ordinary plural.** This is the heart of the unit: one, two, three-four, and five-plus demand four different noun forms. English handles it with just two — "one book, two books, five books" — so this part really does need repeating until it's a reflex.

grammars.title: Numbers 0 to 20
body: Eleven to nineteen all end in **-najst** — one ending, nine numbers. Learn one to ten properly and the rest build themselves.
after: The first four numbers have **gender**: *en brat* but *ena knjiga* but *eno okno*; *dva brata* but *dve knjigi*; *trije bratje* but *tri knjige*; *štirje bratje* but *štiri knjige*. From five on, the numbers stop caring — and that's quite a relief.
The forms ending in *-je* (*trije*, *štirje*) are used **only** for groups of men or mixed groups of people. For things, feminine, and neuter, use *tri* and *štiri*.

grammars.title: Tens and compound numbers
body: Tens are built with *-deset* (from *deset*, ten), and compound numbers are put together back to front with *in* in the middle.
after: Notice that "a hundred" and "a thousand" do **not** use the word "one": *sto*, not *en sto*; *tisoč*, not *en tisoč*. For 200 and up, the number sticks on: *dvesto*, *tristo*, *štiristo*, *petsto*.

The back-to-front order feels strange for a few days, then stops feeling like anything. What matters: when you hear a price or a house number, **listen to the end** — *enaindvajset* and *dvaindvajset* differ only in the first syllable, and a hurried ear often gets it wrong.

grammars.title: Four patterns: number + noun
body: This is the rule that makes Slovenian feel different from every language you've seen. The noun form is decided by the **last number** spoken, not by how big the number is.
after: The last row is a pleasant surprise: since the **last** number decides, *enaindvajset knjiga* takes the singular — 21 ends in "one". Likewise *dvaindvajset knjigi* takes the dual, and *triindvajset knjige* the plural. The system cycles every ten numbers.

The **Genitive plural** used from five up often has no ending at all on feminine words (*knjiga* → *knjig*, *ura* → *ur*, *miza* → *miz*) and ends in *-ov* on masculine words (*brat* → *bratov*, *evro* → *evrov*, *dan* → *dni*). Neuter words usually slip in a vowel: *okno* → *oken*, *mesto* → *mest*, *pismo* → *pisem*.

blocks.text: Numbers are used most for four things: age, quantity, price, and time. The first two are on this page; prices wait in unit 7, telling time in unit 9.

head: Sentence
Say it
Meaning
rows: How old are you? (to a man)
How old are you? (to a woman)

blocks.text: Look at *leto* (year) passing through all four patterns at once: *eno leto* (1), *dve leti* (2), *tri leta* (3), *pet let* (5+). If you only have time to learn one noun in four forms, learn this one — it comes up every time someone asks your age.

*Ljudje* (people) is a word that doesn't play along: its plural is completely different from the singular *človek*, and after five it becomes *ljudi*. *Pet ljudi* = five people. For two people, Slovenians say *dva človeka*.

blocks.title: Reading numbers and dates
items: Phone numbers are read in groups of two or three digits: *nič štiri ena — dve tri — pet šest sedem*.
Years are read whole, not split up as in English: 1991 = *tisoč devetsto enaindevetdeset*, not "nineteen ninety-one".
House numbers and bus numbers are read as one whole number: *avtobus številka dvajset* (bus number twenty).

blocks.text: The following phrases use numbers in the forms you'll hear most often in the street, in shops, and in class.

Note that **veliko** (a lot) and **malo** (a little) behave exactly like numbers from five up: both pull in the Genitive. *Veliko ljudi*, *malo denarja*, *veliko časa* (lots of time). Once you've mastered that form for numbers, you get every quantity word for free.

At the market, *kilogram* is almost always shortened to **kilo** — and *kilo* doesn't change form, so *dva kilo* and *pet kilo* both sound natural. One of the few places where Slovenian gives you a shortcut.
